lesson.title: Freedom as a War Measure: Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation
lesson.summary: Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation, issued in preliminary form after Antietam and made final on January 1, 1863, declared enslaved people in Confederate-held territory free and transformed the Civil War into a fight against slavery itself.
lesson.body:
When the Civil War began in April 1861, Lincoln's stated goal was narrow and specific: preserve the Union, not abolish slavery. He worried, with good reason, that an antislavery war aim would push the slaveholding border states of Maryland, Kentucky, Missouri, and Delaware, all of which had stayed loyal to the Union, into the Confederacy, and he moved cautiously even as abolitionists and many Republicans in Congress pressed him to act. Over 1862, though, the practical and political pressures shifted. Tens of thousands of enslaved people were already fleeing to Union lines and being classified as contraband of war rather than returned to their owners, Congress passed confiscation acts allowing the seizure of enslaved people used to support the rebellion, and Lincoln himself came to see emancipation as a way to weaken the Confederacy's labor force and add moral weight to the Union cause.

Lincoln waited for a Union battlefield success before acting, not wanting the proclamation to look like an act of desperation, and the qualified Union victory at Antietam on September 17, 1862, gave him the moment he needed. Five days later he issued the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation, warning the Confederate states that if they did not return to the Union by January 1, 1863, all enslaved people in the states still in rebellion would be declared free. None of the Confederate states rejoined, and on January 1, 1863, Lincoln signed the final Emancipation Proclamation into effect.

The proclamation's reach was carefully, and controversially, limited. Because Lincoln issued it under his war powers as commander in chief, it applied only to enslaved people in Confederate territory not yet under Union control, meaning it freed no one in the loyal border states and technically freed no one in Confederate areas already occupied by Union troops, since those areas were treated as outside the rebellion. Critics at the time and since have noted the irony that the proclamation, on paper, freed people the Union government had no power to actually reach while leaving untouched people it could have freed immediately. In practice, though, its effect went far beyond its narrow legal wording: it committed the Union to ending slavery wherever its armies advanced, and as Union forces pushed deeper into the Confederacy over the following two years, the proclamation became the legal basis for freeing hundreds of thousands of enslaved people.

The proclamation also authorized the enlistment of Black men into the Union Army and Navy for the first time on a large scale, and roughly 180,000 Black soldiers, along with thousands more in the Navy, ultimately served the Union cause, including celebrated units like the 54th Massachusetts Infantry. Internationally, the proclamation made it politically almost impossible for Britain or France, both of which had already abolished slavery in their own empires, to formally recognize or ally with the Confederacy without appearing to endorse slavery outright. The Emancipation Proclamation did not by itself end slavery everywhere in the United States, that final step came with the Thirteenth Amendment, ratified in December 1865, but it permanently redefined what a Union victory would mean.
